questions.question: Describe the rock art of the Drakensberg and why it is a World Heritage Site.
questions.expected_answer: The Drakensberg, or uKhahlamba, along the KwaZulu-Natal and Lesotho border, has tens of thousands of San paintings at hundreds of sites, one of the largest collections in Africa. They show eland and other animals, people hunting and dancing, and part-human figures, with the newest from the 1800s showing horses and guns. It became a World Heritage Site in 2000 for both its natural beauty and its rock art.

questions.question: Explain how San rock paintings were made and what they may mean.
questions.expected_answer: Artists ground ochre for red, brown and yellow, white clay for white and charcoal for black, mixed with liquids such as blood, fat, egg, plant juice or water, and painted with brushes of feathers, hair or reeds and their fingers, using shading. Many researchers link the art to the spirit world: healers danced into a trance to heal and make rain, and the eland held great power, as the dying eland at Game Pass Shelter may show.

questions.question: Why is rock art fragile, and how is it protected?
questions.expected_answer: Water seeping through the rock, rain, sun, dust, fire smoke and nests can make paintings fade or flake, and people damage them by touching, wetting, graffiti and theft. Once damaged, it is lost forever. The law protects all rock art, making damage or removal a crime, many sites need an accredited guide, rock art centres educate visitors, and researchers record paintings with photos and copies.
